purpose: Track manual, claim-by-claim factual review. Shape validation and automated model review do not count as factual verification.
reviewRequirements: Extract each externally verifiable statement, including versions, APIs, limits, protocol behavior, and safety claims.
Check claims against primary standards, official product documentation, or original research; use the Handbook only for its own curriculum and index contents.
Record each claim, the supporting source URL and relevant section, verdict, and correction when needed.
Check omissions against the frozen manifest and stated topic scope; add missing material before marking a lesson reviewed.
Keep the lesson in drafts until every claim is verified and the required content checks pass.

evidence.claim: DNS is a distributed hierarchical domain-name system; resolvers cache responses subject to DNS TTL information.
A DNS address result does not authenticate the application service identity; service identity verification is a separate TLS/application check.
TCP provides a reliable, ordered byte stream rather than application message boundaries; applications need their own framing.

TLS 1.3 is specified by RFC 9846 (July 2026), which obsoletes RFC 8446 while retaining version 1.3 and backward compatibility; it forbids KeyShare reuse across connections and TLS 1.0/1.1 negotiation.
TLS provides confidentiality, integrity, and peer authentication when the protocol is configured and identity validation is performed; mutual client authentication is optional.
HTTP/1.1 uses persistent connections; requests on a connection are sequential and pipelining can suffer application-level head-of-line blocking.
RFC 9931 (March 2026) adds security requirements for optimistic HTTP/1.1 protocol transitions and CONNECT handling, including protections against forwarding untrusted data before acceptance.
HTTP/2 allows concurrent exchanges on one connection and compresses fields, but TCP packet loss can stall all active transactions sharing that TCP connection.
HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics over QUIC and uses QUIC stream multiplexing; loss on one stream does not block progress on other streams, while congestion control is shared across the connection.
RFC 6455 WebSocket has an opening handshake followed by framed two-way communication; RFC 8441 separately defines WebSocket bootstrapping over HTTP/2 with extended CONNECT.
WebSocket protocol support does not itself supply application authorization, durable replay, or fan-out policy.

The WHATWG EventSource API opens a server-to-client event stream over HTTP and reconnects after closure; Last-Event-ID supports resumption only when the server has and returns corresponding event history.
The lesson’s HTTP/2, HTTP/3, WebSocket, and SSE comparison accurately distinguishes transport/protocol behavior from application authorization, replay, backpressure, and fan-out responsibilities.

evidence.claim: Linearizability requires a legal sequential history that respects real-time precedence of non-overlapping operations.
Sequential consistency requires one legal total order preserving each process's program order, without imposing cross-process real-time order.
evidence.section: Lamport paper definition; contrast with linearizability real-time precedence

evidence.claim: Eventual consistency is a convergence condition under further communication and no continuing writes; it has no inherent finite freshness bound.
evidence.section: Coordination Avoidance report Appendix A.3; Cornell geo-replicated systems notes
evidence.verdict: supported; wording tied to required communication/reconciliation conditions

evidence.claim: Read-your-writes is a per-session guarantee, distinct from atomic transactions or global visibility, and enforcing session guarantees can restrict available servers.
For fixed replica sets, R+W>N implies every read set intersects every write set, but this alone does not establish linearizability without version/order and failure assumptions.
evidence.section: Cassandra tunable consistency; quorum intersection distinction

evidence.claim: Consensus safety and liveness depend on different assumptions; quorum intersection supports safety and an available non-faulty quorum plus synchrony conditions supports progress in the cited Paxos model.
Raft elects a leader, replicates log entries, commits according to majority replication and current-term rules, and cannot commit when a majority is unavailable.
Raft membership changes and log compaction are addressed separately in the paper and matter to correct implementation and operation.
Classical 2PC has prepare/vote and decision phases, and can block prepared participants when coordinator failure leaves them uncertain about the decision.
2PC and consensus are related but distinct protocols; consensus replication of a commit decision is one fault-tolerant commit construction, not a claim that ordinary 2PC is nonblocking consensus.
A microservice-local consensus log does not by itself atomically commit a cross-service workflow; saga compensation has different visible intermediate-state semantics.
evidence.section: Distributed transaction commit distinction; compensating transaction pattern
evidence.verdict: supported; architecture comparison scoped as conceptual

evidence.claim: CAP atomic consistency means each operation appears to occur at one instant between request and response; availability means every request eventually receives a response; communication may delay or lose messages.
CAP’s practical consistency/availability tradeoff is triggered by an actual partition; CAP does not constrain all normal operation choices.
PACELC describes P→A/C during partitions and E→L/C otherwise.
With fixed RF=3 and thresholds R=2,W=2, every read set intersects every write set; this is not alone a proof of linearizability.
Cassandra consistency levels vary response thresholds; ANY is a write-only level that may be satisfied by a stored hint.
Cassandra hinted handoff is best-effort and does not replace anti-entropy repair.
Cassandra 5.0 blocking read repair provides monotonic quorum reads; NONE preserves partition-level write atomicity; both have different tradeoffs.
evidence.section: Read repair settings, BLOCKING and NONE

evidence.claim: Cassandra hints are stored temporarily by coordinators for unavailable replicas; hints and read repair are best-effort, while full or incremental anti-entropy repair addresses broader missed-update cases.
evidence.section: Hints; temporary local storage and convergence mechanisms

evidence.claim: Cassandra repair compares replica data using Merkle trees, streams differences, and is operator-run; one node’s repair does not cover the whole cluster.

evidence.claim: Redis embeds Lua 5.1 for server-side scripting and exposes script keys/arguments through KEYS and ARGV.
Script execution is atomic relative to other Redis commands on the executing server, and blocks those commands while it runs.
Running logic near the data can reduce network round trips for read/decision/write sequences.
evidence.verdict: supported as a design benefit, not a latency guarantee

evidence.claim: Every accessed key must be declared as a key argument; Redis Cluster requires multi-key operations/scripts to use one hash slot.
EVALSHA depends on Redis script-cache presence, and applications must recover if a script is absent.
Redis Functions were added in Redis 7 and provide server-managed libraries that are persisted and replicated.
Redis Functions and Eval scripts both have atomic, blocking execution semantics.
A slow script stalls other work on that Redis server; after writes have occurred it cannot be safely interrupted with SCRIPT KILL.
Redis script atomicity does not provide one transaction spanning Redis and SQL Server or arbitrary cluster shards.
evidence.section: Cluster key-slot scope; Redis transaction scope

evidence.claim: WATCH with MULTI/EXEC implements optimistic conflict detection and clients must handle aborted/retried transactions.
A retry-safe reservation requires application logic to store and enforce a stable reservation/idempotency identifier.
evidence.verdict: supported as a condition; lesson makes enforcement explicit

evidence.claim: Inventory authority, expiry, and reconciliation with a durable order store remain separate design decisions.
This reference is conceptual; exact implementation features and behavior vary by product, version, configuration, and deployment.
evidence.section: EVAL scripts and Redis Functions version/lifecycle differences
evidence.verdict: supported; the lesson labels product/version boundaries and cites the current official profile or specification.

evidence.claim: Starting Redis 7.4, Redis can evict scripts loaded by EVAL/EVAL_RO when its script cache reaches a certain size, so EVALSHA callers must handle cache misses.
evidence.section: EVAL note on script cache eviction since 7.4
evidence.verdict: supported; lesson includes the version boundary and recovery case.

evidence.claim: SQS standard-queue retention clock remains based on original enqueue time after DLQ transfer; FIFO behavior differs.

Transient and permanent failures should not be handled with the same retry policy; backoff and idempotency affect retry safety.
Repeated delivery can duplicate side effects if a prior attempt committed before acknowledgment; idempotency/deduplication addresses repeats.
Bulk redrive can overload a destination or repeat the failure; bounded replay and diagnosis are operational safeguards.
Message acknowledgment and an unrelated database commit are not atomic unless an explicitly supported transaction boundary connects them.

Double Ratchet derives distinct message keys and its DH ratchet can provide recovery after fresh entropy, subject to protocol state and compromise timing.

evidence.claim: Signal safety-number comparison helps verify cryptographic keys but does not establish real-world identity by itself.
Removing a device cannot erase plaintext or keys already copied to that device; future key distribution is a separate lifecycle control.
Backup encryption is a separate boundary and provider-readable plaintext/key backups weaken an endpoint-only content guarantee.
evidence.section: Secure deletion and key storage model

evidence.claim: E2EE limits server-side content processing such as content search/moderation unless those functions are moved to endpoints or use a separately designed mechanism.
evidence.section: Server stores and relays protocol data; endpoint decryption

evidence.claim: HLS delivers live and on-demand media through playlists and media resources over HTTP infrastructure, including web servers and CDNs.
A Multivariant/Master Playlist lists available variants and rendition groups; a Media Playlist describes media segments.
A live Media Playlist is reloaded to discover updates; a VOD playlist describes a finite presentation and can include ENDLIST.
HLS classic RFC 8216 is an August 2017 Informational document describing protocol version 7, not a complete description of all current profiles.
evidence.section: RFC status; Apple maintained authoring specification

evidence.claim: Adaptive switching depends on compatible renditions, timing, codecs, and playlist metadata rather than bitrate entries alone.
Low-Latency HLS is a coordinated origin, packager, CDN, and player feature; reducing segment duration alone does not define the full protocol behavior.
HLS encryption/content protection feature behavior depends on key format and target platform; Apple authoring profile specifies FairPlay requirements.
Media encryption is not equivalent to E2EE because the streaming service generally participates in key delivery, entitlement, or packaging.
evidence.section: Client key fetch and content protection

evidence.claim: MPEG-DASH and HLS both use HTTP adaptive streaming but have distinct manifest/profile interoperability requirements.
CMAF can support shared media packaging workflows across compatible HLS/DASH profiles but does not make every manifest, codec, protection system, or player interchangeable.
evidence.section: DASH CMAF part; HLS CMAF support

evidence.claim: Live streaming design should measure glass-to-glass latency, playback stalls, and recovery rather than infer latency from segment duration alone.
A failure design should provide compatible alternate renditions and verify origin/CDN availability, because playlist references alone cannot guarantee media availability.
